summary.text: In cosmology, the expansion of the universe is the increase in distance between gravitationally unbound parts of the observable universe with time.
Within general relativity it is modeled mathematically with the Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) metric.
The standard Lambda-CDM model hypothesizes different expansion rates at different times, depending on the physical properties of the contents of spacetime.

facts.label: Mathematical model
facts.value: The FLRW metric within general relativity

facts.value: Expansion by a factor of at least 10²⁶

items.prompt: Hubble firmly established the distance and speed relationship in 1929. How did he himself view it?

options.label: He saw it at once as proof that space itself expands
He did not link it to expansion, but his work sparked interest in earlier theory
He believed it showed the universe was shrinking
He presented it as an idea first worked out by Lundmark

items.explain: Hubble did not associate the relationship with expansion, but his publications sparked interest in the earlier theoretical work.

items.prompt: Lundmark's 1924 results were accurate even by today's standards. Why were they not taken as firm evidence then?

options.label: They relied on galaxy diameters and Andromeda's distance, which were unproven
They relied on a telescope that had not yet been built
They relied on a theory that Einstein had rejected
They relied on data collected by a rival astronomer

items.explain: Lundmark's results relied on galaxy diameter measurements and the distance to the Andromeda Galaxy, which were unproven at the time.

items.prompt: In 1927 a physicist applied Einstein's equations to data from Slipher and Hubble. What did he propose?

options.label: A relationship in which distance squared sets speed
A relationship in which speed falls as distance grows
A linear relationship between distance and recessional velocity
A relationship in which speed and distance are unrelated

items.explain: Lemaître derived solutions to Einstein's equations and proposed a linear relationship between distance to galaxies and their recessional velocity.

items.prompt: Expansion is uniform across space. Is it also uniform across long stretches of time?

options.label: Yes, the rate has been exactly the same since the start
No, the rate is zero at all times except the present
Yes, the rate changes only inside gravitationally bound regions
No, the rate varies with time, and that variation is a central object of study

items.explain: While expansion in space is uniform, the rate varies with time and this variation is a central object of study in cosmology.

items.prompt: What did the 1994 repair of the Hubble Space Telescope's main mirror change for measuring the expansion?

options.label: It allowed the telescope to be pointed at a wider patch of sky
It allowed sharper images and more accurate analyses of its observations
It removed the need for any ground-based measurements
It made the telescope able to see the earliest galaxies

items.explain: The repairs allowed sharper images and more accurate analyses, and shortly after, Freedman's Key Project offered a Hubble constant measurement.

items.prompt: In the standard model of cosmology, what decides how fast space expands at a given time?

options.label: The physical properties of the contents of spacetime
The age of the oldest star in the observable universe
The number of galaxies that are bound by gravity
The speed at which light crosses the universe

paragraphs.heading: What expansion means
paragraphs.text: The expansion of the universe is the growth, over time, of the distance between parts of the observable universe that gravity does not hold together. It is built into space itself: the universe is not swelling into some outside region, and there is no space beyond it. Galaxies near enough to be bound by gravity stay together. But from any vantage point, nearly every other galaxy seems on average to be moving away, and the farther off it is, the faster it goes.

paragraphs.heading: Faster than light, yet allowed
paragraphs.text: Nothing can travel faster than light, but that rule only holds within a local frame of reference. It sets no cap on how quickly very distant objects recede from one another. The idea is hard to explain, and that has led to several common misunderstandings about what expansion is, where it came from and what it does.

paragraphs.heading: How it was found
paragraphs.text: In the 1920s, theory and observation arrived at expansion separately. Between 1912 and 1914, Vesto Slipher saw that light from far galaxies was shifted toward the red, which was later read as those galaxies moving away from Earth. In 1922, Alexander Friedmann used Einstein's field equations to argue on theoretical grounds that the universe is growing. In 1927, Georges Lemaître applied general relativity to data from Slipher and Hubble and proposed a straight-line link between a galaxy's distance and its speed away from us, and Edwin Hubble placed that link on firm ground in 1929.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the rate
paragraphs.text: The pace of expansion today is captured by a single number, the Hubble constant, written H₀. Space expands evenly from place to place, but the rate shifts over time, and tracking that shift is a central task of cosmology. Through much of the later twentieth century, estimates of the constant sat between 50 and 90 km⋅s⁻¹⋅Mpc⁻¹. In 2003, an analysis of the cosmic microwave background from the WMAP satellite's first year gave 72±5 km⋅s⁻¹⋅Mpc⁻¹, agreeing with values found from nearby galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: A pace that changes
paragraphs.text: The standard model of cosmology, called Lambda-CDM, holds that the rate has differed from era to era, depending on what fills spacetime. In the very first stage, called inflation, when the universe was only about 10⁻³² of a second old, it suddenly grew at least 10²⁶ times over in every direction. After that the growth slowed a great deal. Then, roughly 9.8 billion years after the Big Bang, or about 4 billion years ago, it began to speed up gradually, and it still is. To explain this recent speeding up, physicists have proposed dark energy, which in the simplest models appears as a cosmological constant and is expected to dominate the future.

paragraphs.heading: The scale factor
paragraphs.text: In the mathematics, expansion is tracked with the scale factor, a, a number proportional to the typical spacing between objects such as galaxies. It changes with time and is set to a = 1 today, so it was smaller in the past and will be larger in the future. Running the clock backward in some models reaches a moment when a was zero, which current cosmology places 13.787 ± 0.020 billion years ago. If expansion goes on forever, a grows without limit, though in principle the universe could instead stop and start to shrink, with a falling over time.
